notes.h: Concepts of physical activity: from everyday movement to school and leisure
notes.b: Physical activity is the broad idea, and it runs on a continuum, from healthy-lifestyle activity at one end to competing to win at the other. Play, leisure and recreation, and physical education sit at the relaxed and learning end, and each has its own purpose.
points: Physical activity is any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles (the muscles attached to your bones) that uses energy, so it covers everything from a walk to school to a professional match.

Play is spontaneous, freely chosen activity done for its own sake, with flexible or self-made rules, and it is mainly associated with children. Examples: chasing games in a playground; kicking a ball around a park with self-made goals.

Leisure and recreation is activity chosen in free time for enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, with little emphasis on competition, because the point is to feel good rather than to win. Examples: a walk; a leisurely cycle; a swim.

Physical education is planned, structured learning in, through and about physical activity within the school curriculum, taught by a qualified teacher. Examples: a PE class learning the technique of a striking action; a lesson on how the body responds to exercise.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define or explain each concept and to match concepts to descriptions with examples. Give the key features (free choice for play, a qualified teacher and the curriculum for PE) and two examples each.

notes.h: Concepts of physical activity: mass participation, outdoor and adventure, and sport
notes.b: At the organised end of the continuum are events and activities with a set structure. They differ in their purpose: personal challenge, adventure in nature, or winning.
points: Mass-participation sports are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge or charity rather than to win. Examples: city marathons; fun runs; sportives; parkrun.
parkrun is a free, weekly, timed 5 km event held on Saturday mornings in many locations and open to everyone, which makes it a clear example of many people of mixed ability taking part together.
Outdoor and adventure activities take place in the natural environment and involve challenge, managed risk (risk that is assessed and controlled) and uncertainty.
Land-based outdoor and adventure activities: hill walking, orienteering, rock-climbing and mountain biking.
Water-based outdoor and adventure activities: canoeing, kayaking, sailing and surfing.

Sport is organised, competitive physical activity governed by formal rules and a governing body, with an emphasis on performance and winning. Examples: a club league in Gaelic football; a national championship in swimming.
notes.tip: Mass-participation sport is about many participants at once, not about popularity on television. If asked for outdoor and adventure activities other than water activities, leave out canoeing, kayaking, sailing, rowing and surfing and name land-based ones such as hill walking, orienteering, rock-climbing and mountain biking.

notes.b: Regular activity keeps the heart, bones and body systems working well. This is why it protects against many long-term illnesses and makes daily life easier.
points: Lower risk of heart disease and stroke, because activity keeps the heart and circulation working well.
Lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
Lower risk of obesity, which supports weight management because activity uses energy.
Lower risk of some cancers.
Stronger bones and a lower risk of osteoporosis (a condition in which bones become weak and break easily).
Better fitness, which makes everyday physical tasks easier.
Better sleep.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to identify four benefits of participation or to give personal benefits. Name specific ones, such as a lower risk of heart disease, stronger bones, better fitness and better sleep, rather than just saying 'being healthier'.

notes.b: Physical activity helps the mind as well as the body. It affects how people feel, think and stay motivated.
points: Improved mood and self-esteem (how you value yourself).
Reduced stress and anxiety.
Reduced symptoms of depression.
Better concentration.
Enjoyment and a sense of achievement, which sustain motivation to keep taking part, so people carry on being active.
notes.tip: Keep personal benefits separate from social and economic ones. Mood, stress, anxiety and self-esteem are mental benefits, while fitter bones and a healthier heart are physical benefits.

notes.b: Most physical activity involves other people. This is why it can build relationships, skills and communities as well as fitness.
points: Making friends and belonging to a group, which come from regularly taking part alongside the same people.
Teamwork, communication and leadership skills develop through group activity, because people must work together, talk to each other and sometimes take charge.
A social outlet and a positive use of free time.
Reduced isolation, because activity brings people together regularly.
Community cohesion (people in a community getting along and sticking together), as people from different backgrounds meet through shared activity.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to outline social benefits for teenagers or adults. Write about relationships, teamwork, belonging and community, and keep fitness out of it.

notes.b: Economic benefits are about money. They fall on society as a whole and on the individual, and a student should keep the two apart.
points: For society: lower healthcare costs, because fewer people need treatment.
For society: fewer sick days and higher productivity at work, because healthier workers are absent less.
For society: employment in the sport and leisure industry.
For society: income from tourism and events.
For society: the value of volunteering, which keeps clubs and events running.
For the individual: lower medical costs, since fewer treatments are needed.
For the individual: career opportunities in coaching, officiating (acting as a referee or umpire), teaching and the leisure industry.
For the individual: free activities such as walking cost less than health treatment for conditions that inactivity can cause.
notes.tip: Economic benefits are financial, not 'fitter people'. Write about costs saved, jobs and income, and keep the three types of benefit (personal, social, economic) distinct.

notes.h: Benefits by life stage: children and adolescents
notes.b: The benefits of activity change with age. In childhood and the teenage years it helps the body develop and shapes habits and confidence.
points: Children: motor-skill development, such as running, jumping, throwing and catching.
Children: healthy growth, supported by play and daily activity.
Children: social skills learned through play with others.
Adolescents (teenagers): self-esteem and body image, which are formed during the teenage years.
Adolescents: stress relief during the pressures of school and exams.
Adolescents: friendships and belonging to a peer group (people of the same age).
Adolescents: lifelong habits that can carry into adult life, because activity habits set in the teenage years tend to last.
notes.tip: Questions ask for benefits for children and for teenagers separately. Match each to the stage: motor skills and growth through play for children; self-esteem, body image, stress, friendships and habits for teenagers.

notes.h: Benefits by life stage: adults and older adults
notes.b: Adults use activity to protect their health and manage pressure. For older adults it also protects independence and the ability to move safely.
points: Adults: weight and disease prevention, which protects health across working life.
Adults: stress relief from work and family demands.
Adults: social contact outside work.
Adults: work productivity, which keeps people able to meet job demands.
Older adults: balance and strength, which help prevent falls.
Older adults: bone density, which helps protect against fractures.
Older adults: independence in daily life for longer.
Older adults: social contact and reduced loneliness, and cognitive health (thinking and memory).
notes.tip: For health benefits for older adults, link each benefit to its result: balance and strength prevent falls, and bone density protects against fractures. Exams may also ask for named activities.

notes.b: Get Ireland Active sets the national activity guidelines. They say how much activity each age group needs to gain the benefits above.
points: Children and young people: at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day.
Adults: at least 30 minutes of moderate activity on five days a week, which is 150 minutes a week.
Older adults: the adult target of 30 minutes of moderate activity on five days a week, plus balance and strength activities, which target the falls and fracture risks of older age.

questions.prompt: Discuss the personal benefits of physical activity for health and wellbeing for people at two different life stages.
questions.model: Adolescents: physical benefits include a lower risk of heart disease and better fitness, and activity helps build lifelong habits that can carry into adulthood. Mental benefits include improved mood, higher self-esteem and relief from the stress of school and exams, which matters most in the teenage years. Friendships and a sense of belonging through team and club activity also support wellbeing at this stage. Older adults: physical benefits include balance and strength that help prevent falls, bone density that helps protect against fractures, and independence in daily life for longer. Mental benefits include reduced stress and anxiety, fewer symptoms of depression and better concentration, while social contact reduces isolation and loneliness and supports cognitive health. The emphasis differs between the stages: for teenagers, self-esteem, body image and habit formation matter most, while for older adults the focus shifts to preventing falls, protecting bone health and staying independent.

questions.prompt: Discuss two economic benefits of physical activity participation.
questions.model: Lower healthcare costs: regular activity reduces the need for treatment for conditions such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes, so the state spends less on healthcare. For the individual, a free activity such as walking costs less than health treatment. Employment and income: the sport and leisure industry employs coaches, instructors and event staff, and events and tourism bring money into an area. Volunteering also keeps clubs running without wage costs. Fewer sick days and higher productivity at work further reduce the cost of absence for employers and the wider economy.

questions.prompt: Explain the concepts 'play' and 'mass-participation sports', giving an example of each.
questions.model: Play is spontaneous, freely chosen activity done for its own sake, with flexible or self-made rules, and is mainly associated with children. Example: chasing games in a playground, where the children change the rules as they go. Mass-participation sports are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for a personal challenge or charity rather than to win. Example: a city marathon, where runners of all abilities complete the same course together.
